extracted.intended_audience: general readers, performing-arts historians, and practitioners interested in the history and practice of vaudeville/variety performance
extracted.subtask_description: Historical/practical standards and conventions for assembling and running vaudeville (variety) shows: show structure, booking/circuit practices, censorship norms, audience targeting, and venue/act-level expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety-show structure (series of separate, unrelated acts)
rubrics_metrics.description: A typical North American vaudeville performance was made up of a series of separate, unrelated acts grouped together on a common bill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Types of acts included popular and classical musicians, singers, dancers, comedians, trained animals, magicians, ventriloquists, strongmen, impersonators, acrobats, clowns, mimes, illustrated songs, jugglers, athletes, lecturing celebrities, scenes from plays, one-act plays, minstrels, and films. The multi-act/variety format—unrelated acts on a single bill—is a defining structural standard for vaudeville shows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polite Vaudeville / family-friendly standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A more genteel form, known as 'Polite Vaudeville', committed to entertainment equally inoffensive to men, women and children; managers barred sale of liquor and eliminated bawdy material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implemented by impresarios such as Tony Pastor and promoted across major circuits: exclude bawdy material, make programs family-appropriate, and tailor theatre policies (e.g., no liquor) to attract middle-class and family audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard bill sequencing / placement of acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical pattern: open with a 'dumb' act to allow patrons to find seats, place strong acts in second and penultimate positions, and leave the weakest act for the end to clear the house.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bill examples show intentional ordering to manage audience attention and flow—use weaker, non-disruptive openings, concentrate highlights near the beginning and before the finale, and end with a spectacle or final extravaganza.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managerial censorship and enforcement practices (the 'blue envelopes' system)
rubrics_metrics.description: Managers (notably B. F. Keith) enforced strict standards backstage: posted warnings about prohibited words and issued 'blue envelopes' directing the omission or substitution of suggestive lines; failure to comply could earn a 'black mark' and effective blacklisting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Censorship was formalized: explicit backstage rules, written orders about lines to remove, and career-level penalties for noncompliance. This produced a culture where performers learned to follow managerial instructions to avoid losing bookings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circuits and standardized booking as industrial practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Vaudeville circuits contracted acts for regional and national tours, standardizing booking and enabling engagements to be lengthened from a few weeks to years; circuits remedied chaotic single-theatre booking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major circuits (e.g., Keith-Albee, Orpheum, Pantages) provided the industry's principal economic and organizational structure. Acts were booked centrally, enabling predictable touring schedules, career progression, and economies of scale for managers and performers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Levels of the vaudeville circuit: small time, medium time, big time
rubrics_metrics.description: Three common levels determined pay, frequency, and venue type: 'small time' (lower-paying, rougher venues, frequent performances), 'medium time' (moderate wages, two performances per day in purpose-built theatres), and 'big time' (high pay, large urban theatres catering to middle/upper-middle classes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performers aspired to advance through these tiers as they gained renown; expectations about remuneration, venue quality, touring rigour, and audience demographics varied by level.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Will it play in Peoria?' — mainstream-appeal metric
rubrics_metrics.description: A popularly cited test of an act's commercial viability: if an act would succeed in Peoria, Illinois, it would work anywhere—used as a metaphor for mainstream American appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts and managers used broad-audience appeal (rather than niche or avant-garde material) as a key criterion when evaluating the likely commercial success of a routine on national circuits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting demographic-specific circuits and tailoring material
rubrics_metrics.description: Mature vaudeville featured houses and circuits aimed at specific demographic groups (e.g., Black patrons, Italian- or Yiddish-speaking audiences); material was tailored to those audiences and segregation shaped bookings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Black performers often toured on separate circuits or had restricted placement on white-oriented bills; ethnic-language circuits and targeted programming allowed acts to connect with particular communities and cultivate niche followings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'blue' (sexual/scandalous) material as a marketing strategy vs censorship tension
rubrics_metrics.description: Managers sometimes used scandalous or sexual ('blue') material to attract audiences and increase revenue, even while other managers (and circuits) formally censored such content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This created tension: some houses sanitized shows to be 'polite', while others exploited risqué material for box-office draw. Practitioners needed to balance market demand against circuit rules and potential blacklisting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of cinema into vaudeville programming / performer transition to film
rubrics_metrics.description: Cinema was incorporated into vaudeville shows early on; as films (especially talking pictures) grew, managers added cinema, and many performers transitioned to film for higher pay and less arduous conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inclusion of motion pictures in programs became a strategic choice for managers; the arrival of talking pictures in the late 1920s critically altered vaudeville's competitive position and was a major structural factor in its decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixing of 'highbrow' and 'lowbrow' acts on the same bill
rubrics_metrics.description: Vaudeville bills commonly juxtaposed acts regarded as 'lowbrow' (acrobats, trained animals) with 'highbrow' acts (opera vocalists, classical musicians) on the same program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curate bills to combine diverse appeal—pair novelty or mass-appeal acts with displays of recognized artistry to broaden audience interest and legitimize variety programming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue scale and theatre-architecture considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Programming and production values varied by venue: big-time urban palaces with sophisticated architecture and large houses versus small-time converted saloons or Grange Halls with modest stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose and design acts appropriate to venue size and audience expectations; lavish spectacles and large-company finales suited big urban houses, while intimate or rougher acts fit small-town converted halls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record-keeping and managerial evaluation (report books)
rubrics_metrics.description: Managers maintained report books recording and commenting on each night's lineup and the perceived quality of acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic documentation of nightly performances informed booking decisions, quality control, and career consequences for performers; archives of these records were principal managerial tools for evaluating acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ethnic caricature and immigrant humor as content
rubrics_metrics.description: Vaudeville frequently drew on ethnic stereotypes and immigrant caricatures (e.g., 'greenhorn' Irish, Chinese, Italian, Jewish caricatures) as sources of humor and as ways for immigrant performers to interpret cultural identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While such material helped acts connect with or comment on immigrant experiences and could serve as assimilative or economic strategies, it also perpetuated crude stereotypes and racial hierarchies—an important historical constraint and ethical consideration for modern interpretation.
